docs.title: STCM — Synoptic Transform Calibration Model
docs.text: Welcome to the documentation for the Synoptic Transform Calibration Model, a computational research framework for investigating the Synoptic Problem through NLP embedding analysis.

docs.title: What is this?
docs.text: STCM tests whether a transformer representation of Koine Greek can measure literary dependence — first on relations that are known (Matthew and Luke copying Mark), then on the disputed double tradition (passages found in Matthew and Luke but absent from Mark), and asks what it adds to counting shared words.

docs.title: How does it work?
docs.text:
graph TD
    A[SBLGNT Greek Text] --> B[Koine-Greek-BERT Embeddings]
    B --> C[Triple-Tradition Calibration]
    C --> D[Two-step: Matt-Luke]
    C --> E[One-step: Luke-Mark, Matt-Mark]
    D --> F[Double tradition: excess over own floor]
    E --> F
    F --> H[Permutation nulls, CIs, Mark-Q overlaps, sayings control]
    F --> J[Lexical baselines: Jaccard, TF-IDF]
    F --> G[Covariates & directionality controls]
    J --> I
    G --> I[Results & Reports]
    H --> I

docs.title: Does STCM prove that Q existed?
docs.text: No. Computational linguistics cannot "prove" the historical existence of a lost document, and STCM does not try to. What it shows is that a contextual representation of Koine Greek passes positive and negative controls drawn from known dependence (Matthew and Luke copying Mark), and that, measured against those controls, Matthew–Luke agreement in the double tradition is closer than two-step Markan copying and at least as close as one-step copying. That is consistent with close written dependence of some kind — a shared source or Luke's direct use of Matthew — and the method cannot discriminate between the two.

docs.title: Why use Koine-Greek-BERT?
docs.text: Contextual models represent each word in the light of its passage, so they can in principle recognise when Matthew and Luke say the same thing in different words. Whether they actually do is tested rather than assumed: the model must pass the triple-tradition positive control, and its increment over plain word overlap is measured directly (see the next question). Koine-Greek-BERT is domain-adapted on Koine (LXX, NT, Apostolic Fathers, historians); the central result is replicated with Ancient-Greek-BERT, which was not trained on the New Testament.

docs.title: Doesn't the statistic just measure word overlap?
docs.text: Largely, yes — and the project now says so. Word overlap (multiset Jaccard) reproduces most of the ranking (Spearman ρ = 0.87) and the same ordering of the traditions. What the embedding adds is measured in baselines.py: after removing the linear effect of word overlap, the residual still separates true parallels from mismatched pairs (p < 0.001 against all nulls), and the passages the embedding rates higher than their word overlap predicts are paraphrases (Conditions of Discipleship, One Taken, One Left, the Golden Rule, the Lord's Prayer). The increment is modest but real.

docs.title: What about the circularity problem — aren't similar topics naturally similar?
docs.text: This was addressed with the thematic-null permutation test. Instead of pairing Matt–Luke pericopes randomly, this test pairs each Matthean pericope with a thematically similar Lukan pericope (wisdom with wisdom, apocalyptic with apocalyptic, etc.). The correctly paired pericopes still significantly exceed this thematic baseline (empirical p < 0.001, 1,000 permutations), showing that the signal reflects genuine textual correspondence beyond mere topical similarity. A second kind of circularity is length: true parallels are of similar length, random pairs are not, and unrelated passages of different lengths are less similar than unrelated passages of equal length. Two further nulls therefore pair each Matthean pericope with a Lukan one of comparable length (optionally also of the same theme); the signal survives both (p < 0.001).

docs.title: Are the results sensitive to tuning?
docs.text: The mean-centred cosine has no weights or free parameters. The analytical choices that remain are tested: the centring vector (six definitions — the double-versus-triple ordering holds in all six; the double-versus-Luke–Mark ordering does not), the layer (last vs mean of last four), the encoder (Koine-Greek-BERT vs Ancient-Greek-BERT) and the encoding of composite units (range-wise vs single sequence; individual pericopes move by up to 0.14, corpus-level contrasts do not change sign). An earlier weighted composite index is retired and survives only as a legacy output.

docs.title: What if I don't have internet access to download the model?
docs.text: STCM includes an offline fallback, but it must be enabled explicitly. If ABeZet/Koine-Greek-BERT cannot be loaded via the transformers library, the pipeline stops with an error unless STCM_ALLOW_FALLBACK=1 is set, in which case a deterministic character-trigram hashing embedder (256-dimensional) is used. The fallback is sufficient to demonstrate that the pipeline runs end-to-end, but its results are not comparable to the published outputs; the embedder actually used is recorded in system_validation.txt.

docs.title: What is the Farrer Hypothesis and does STCM disprove it?
docs.text: The Farrer Hypothesis argues that Luke used Matthew as a source, meaning there is no "Q". STCM does not directly falsify this model. However, a Goulder redaction test compares pericopes that Goulder (1989) identifies as demonstrating Lukan redaction of Matthew against the rest. These pericopes show no statistically significant difference in centred-cosine distribution (Welch's t = −1.49, p = 0.17), but the test is underpowered (n = 10 vs. n = 41) and the medium-to-large effect size (Cohen's d = −0.75) indicates a potentially meaningful difference that the current sample cannot confirm or rule out. The result is therefore genuinely inconclusive — it neither supports nor refutes either hypothesis. A direct directionality test (which evangelist's embeddings predict the other's better, by leave-one-out ridge regression) was also built and controlled: it finds a small asymmetry in the double tradition, but the asymmetry depends on the ridge penalty, vanishes among pairs of equal length, and — decisively — the same statistic does not recover the known direction of copying where Matthew and Luke copy Mark. A method that fails its positive control is not allowed to answer the question, so STCM draws no directional inference.

docs.title: What about the minor agreements?
docs.text: They are visible in the geometry. In the triple tradition, what Matthew does to Mark and what Luke does to Mark are correlated pericope by pericope (0.364 against 0.058 for mismatched pericopes, p < 0.001). The geometry cannot tell whether this reflects Luke's knowledge of Matthew or coincident redaction of the same Markan text.

docs.title: What about the possibility that Q was in Aramaic?
docs.text: Casey (2002) argues that Q may have been composed in Aramaic and translated independently into Greek. If so, the Greek-language embeddings would capture two independent translation events rather than the original source. This would attenuate the signal (making significant results more noteworthy, not less) and could explain why some pericopes score lower than expected despite being considered core Q material. It is also worth noting that a Koine Greek BERT model may be sensitive to the distinctive syntax of "translation Greek" — Semitisms and Aramaisms that arise when Greek renders Semitic source constructions. If Matthew and Luke translated an Aramaic Q independently, the resulting variance in Greek syntax would naturally lower cosine similarity, which is consistent with the spectrum of centred cosines observed across the double tradition.

docs.title: Does passage length or literary form drive the ranking?
docs.text: Length does not: the correlation between centred cosine and length in characters is essentially zero (r = 0.002). Literary form shows a pattern — discourses highest, parables lowest — but it is not statistically significant within the double tradition (Kruskal–Wallis p = 0.093). Across traditions, however, the kind of material matters: sayings-dominant triple-tradition units agree more closely than narrative ones, and part of the double tradition's advantage over two-step Markan copying is a sayings-versus-narrative effect (form_control.py).

docs.title: How were the pericopes delimited?
docs.text: By the Aland synopsis and the IQP inventory, under four rules enforced by the loader: each pair is trimmed to the verses that are actually parallel (non-contiguous ranges such as Luke 3:7–9 + 16–17 are supported); no verse belongs to two units of the same set; no verse of Matthew or Luke belongs to both the calibration and the test set (Mark–Q overlaps are excluded from calibration); and a calibration unit must be the Markan episode itself in each gospel. The table has 51 double-tradition and 45 triple-tradition units; 16 double-tradition units with a Markan parallel are flagged and the results reported with and without them. The article shows, with John's Preaching, how much a wrong boundary can move a single pericope (rank 47 with Luke 3:7–9 alone, rank 20 with 3:7–9 + 16–17).

docs.title: Can I run this on John or the non-canonical gospels?
docs.text: Yes, the pipeline can be adapted to any Greek text, but you will need to map the pericopes in data_loader.py (and add their metadata in stcm/metadata.py). Currently, it uses a hardcoded table based on the Aland Synopsis and the IQP inventory for the synoptic gospels.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Python 3.11, 3.12, or 3.13
  • Git
  • uv (recommended) — or pip

docs.title: 1. Clone the repository
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/stcm-research/stcm.git
cd stcm

docs.title: 2. Create a virtual environment and install dependencies
docs.text:
With uv (recommended):

uv venv
uv pip install -r requirements.txt

Or with pip:

python -m venv .venv
# Windows:
.venv\Scripts\activate
# macOS/Linux:
source .venv/bin/activate
pip install -r requirements.txt

docs.title: 3. Download the SBLGNT text
docs.text:
The SBL Greek New Testament text is required. It will be downloaded from the Logos Bible Software GitHub repository.

python download_sblgnt.py

This places matthew.txt, mark.txt, and luke.txt in data/raw/.

You are now ready to run the STCM pipeline.

docs.title: 1. Data and alignment
docs.text:
Greek text: SBLGNT, with its inline critical-apparatus sigla removed. Pericopes follow the Aland synopsis; the double tradition follows the IQP inventory. Four rules are enforced by stcm/data_loader.py:

  1. each pair is trimmed to the verses that are actually parallel (non-contiguous ranges are allowed, e.g. Luke 3:7–9 + 16–17);
  2. no verse belongs to two units of the same set;
  3. no Matthew or Luke verse belongs to both sets; Mark–Q overlaps are excluded from the calibration set;
  4. a calibration unit must be the Markan episode itself in each gospel (Luke 5:1–11 is excluded; the Nazareth sermon is restricted to Luke 4:16, 22, 24).

Result: 45 triple-tradition units (positive control) and 51 double-tradition units (test set), 16 of which have a Markan parallel to all or part of their text (MARK_Q_OVERLAP in stcm/metadata.py).

docs.title: 2. Representation
docs.text:
• Model: ABeZet/Koine-Greek-BERT, pinned to revision b81172e (v1.0.1). Its normaliser lower-cases and strips diacritics, so inference is on unaccented text.
  • Each contiguous verse range is encoded as one sequence; the passage vector is the attention-masked mean of the last hidden layer, L2-normalised.
  • Composite units are encoded range by range and averaged with token-count weights, so the model never sees a splice the evangelist did not write. Texts over 512 tokens are chunked at sentence boundaries and combined the same way. Nothing is truncated.
  • Cache keys include model, revision, layer setting, accent handling and encoding version (v3).

docs.title: 3. Primary statistic
docs.text: The mean-centred cosine cos(x − μ, y − μ), with μ the mean of all 237 pericope vectors. Centring corrects the anisotropy of contextual embeddings (unrelated pairs fall from ≈ 0.84 to ≈ 0.05). The raw cosine is reported in parallel.

docs.title: 4. Floors, excess and uncertainty
docs.text:
For each matched pair, the mean floor is the average similarity of the left text to all non-parallel right texts, and the nearest-neighbour floor the maximum. The evidential quantity is the per-pericope excess over the floor, computed for four sets:

Set What it calibrates Double tradition, Matt–Luke the disputed relation Triple tradition, Matt–Luke two independent copies of one source (two-step) Triple tradition, Luke–Mark and Matt–Mark a copy and its source (one-step)

Set means carry bootstrap CIs over pericopes; differences carry a bootstrap CI, a Mann–Whitney test and a label-permutation test. The nearest-neighbour comparison is repeated with the larger set subsampled to the smaller.

docs.title: 5. Controls and robustness
docs.text:
• Permutation nulls (double tradition): random, thematic (7 categories), length-matched (|log length ratio| ≤ 0.4), length-and-theme-matched; 1,000 draws each.
  • Mark–Q overlaps: double-tradition statistics with and without the 16 overlap units.
  • Kind of material (form_control.py): 11 sayings-dominant triple-tradition units against the double tradition.
  • Centring vector: six alternatives (Table 4 of the article).
  • Encoder (robustness.py): Koine-Greek-BERT mean of last four layers; Ancient-Greek-BERT (not trained on the NT).
  • Composite encoding: range-wise vs single-sequence (composite_sensitivity.csv).

docs.title: 6. Lexical baselines (baselines.py)
docs.text: Multiset Jaccard on accent-stripped word forms and character 3–5-gram TF-IDF cosine are run through the identical floor/excess/null pipeline. The centred-cosine pair matrix is regressed on the Jaccard matrix over all Matthew–Luke pairs and the residual is tested for matched-vs-mismatched separation; the pericopes on which the measures disagree most are listed in baseline_disagreements.csv.

docs.title: 7. Shared deviation from Mark
docs.text: For each triple-tradition pericope, the residual of Matthew's vector orthogonal to Mark's is correlated with Luke's; mismatched-pair floor and random/length-matched nulls as above. This is the geometric counterpart of the minor agreements.

docs.title: 8. Covariates
docs.text: Length (characters), five form classes, Kloppenborg strata (pericope-level approximation), the Goulder set, word overlap, and a sentence-level bootstrap (200 resamples; pericopes with fewer than two sentences in either version are excluded).

docs.title: 9. Directionality
docs.text: Kernel ridge with intercept in both directions, exact leave-one-out R² via the hat-matrix identity, penalty chosen by LOO error, jackknife CI, sign-flip permutation test, a penalty sweep, a length-balanced subset, and the known-direction control (Mark → Matthew, Mark → Luke). The statistic fails that control, so no directional inference is drawn.

docs.title: Legacy
docs.text: The composite Q-score (0.8 × cosine + 0.2 × residual) and the latent-Q reconstruction are retired and run only with run_pipeline.py --legacy.

docs.title: Results
docs.text: All figures on this page are from the version-3 run (October 2026): 51 double-tradition and 45 triple-tradition pericopes, range-wise encoding of composite units, the model pinned to Koine-Greek-BERT v1.0.1. Earlier figures (version 2: 46 triple-tradition pericopes, matched mean 0.7171; version 1: 36/49 pericopes) are superseded. Every number is in outputs/reports/ and key_stats*.json.

docs.title: 1. Positive and negative controls
docs.text:
In the triple tradition, where Matthew and Luke both copy Mark, the mean-centred cosine is 0.578 between Matthew and Luke (two independent copies of one source) and 0.679 / 0.651 between Matthew and Mark / Luke and Mark (a copy and its source). Two independent copies agree less with each other than each does with its source, as they should. Mismatched pairs fall to ≈ 0.05 in every set after centring (raw cosine of unrelated passages ≈ 0.84–0.91). The representation passes both controls.

The 51 double-tradition matched pairs average 0.708 (SD 0.175, range 0.142–0.979) against a mismatched floor of 0.052, and exceed four permutation nulls — random 0.064, thematic 0.110, length-matched 0.086, length-and-theme-matched 0.132 — with p < 0.001 in every case. The uncorrected cosine is concordant (0.950 against nulls of 0.841–0.854).

docs.title: 2. Comparing the traditions — excess over each set's own floor
docs.text:
Set Excess over mean floor, centred [95% CI] raw [95% CI] Double tradition, Matt–Luke 0.656 [0.609, 0.702] 0.112 [0.102, 0.120] Triple tradition, Matt–Luke (two-step copying) 0.525 [0.475, 0.574] 0.052 [0.046, 0.058] Triple tradition, Luke–Mark (one-step copying) 0.586 [0.540, 0.635] 0.059 [0.054, 0.065] Triple tradition, Matt–Mark (one-step copying) 0.609 [0.570, 0.650] 0.058 [0.053, 0.063]
  • Double minus two-step copying: +0.131 [0.063, 0.200] centred, +0.060 [0.050, 0.071] raw — robust: it holds against the nearest-neighbour floor, with the double tradition size-matched, without the 16 Mark–Q overlap units (+0.142), under all six centring vectors, with the last-four-layer encoding and with Ancient-Greek-BERT, which has not seen the New Testament.
  • Double minus one-step copying (Luke–Mark): +0.053 [0.042, 0.063] raw, but only +0.070 [0.004, 0.141] centred, and not stable across centring vectors or encoders. The safe statement: Matthew and Luke agree in the double tradition at least as closely as Luke agrees with Mark where he copies him.
  • Kind of material: the double tradition is mostly sayings, the triple tradition mostly narrative. Against the 11 sayings-dominant triple-tradition units the centred advantage shrinks to +0.077 [−0.061, 0.230], and against Luke–Mark copying of the same units it vanishes (−0.036). In the uncorrected space it persists (+0.060, +0.041). Part of the two-step contrast is a sayings-versus-narrative effect.

docs.title: 3. What the embedding adds to word overlap
docs.text:
Plain word overlap (multiset Jaccard) and character n-gram TF-IDF reproduce the same ordering (Jaccard excess: double 0.313, two-step 0.167, Luke–Mark 0.214) and most of the ranking (Spearman ρ = 0.87 with the centred cosine). The headline contrast is not specific to the transformer.

What is specific: after regressing the centred cosine on Jaccard over all 2,601 Matthew–Luke pairs, the residual still separates matched pairs (+0.180) from mismatched ones (−0.004), p < 0.001 against all nulls, and the double tradition's advantage survives on the residual (+0.085 [0.021, 0.147]). The pericopes the embedding rates higher than their word overlap predicts are cases of paraphrase — Conditions of Discipleship ("loves … more than me / is not worthy of me" against "does not hate … / cannot be my disciple"), One Taken, One Left, the Golden Rule, the Lord's Prayer.

docs.title: 4. Ranking and covariates
docs.text:
Top 5: Serving Two Masters (0.979), Harvest Plentiful (0.955), Lament over Jerusalem (0.944), Hidden from Wise, Revealed (0.915), Return of Unclean Spirit (0.908). Bottom: Narrow Gate (0.142), Great Banquet (0.205).

  • Length: Pearson r = 0.002 (p = 0.99).
  • Form: discourse 0.785 > narrative 0.743 > proverbial 0.683 > parable 0.575, but Kruskal–Wallis p = 0.093 and no pairwise difference survives correction — a pattern, not a finding.
  • Kloppenborg strata: Q¹ 0.714 vs Q² 0.713 (p = 0.97).
  • Goulder set: 0.607 vs 0.733 (p = 0.17, d = −0.75) — underpowered, inconclusive.
  • Sentence-level bootstrap: median per-pericope SD 0.117 (mean 0.133, 47 pericopes with ≥ 2 sentences in each version).

docs.title: 5. Shared deviation from Mark (minor agreements)
docs.text: In the triple tradition, the component of Matthew's vector orthogonal to Mark's correlates with Luke's at 0.364, against 0.058 for mismatched pericopes (random null 0.065, length-matched null 0.063, p < 0.001). Where Matthew and Luke both depart from Mark, they tend to depart in the same direction in the same pericope — the geometric trace of the minor agreements. The geometry cannot say whether this reflects Luke's knowledge of Matthew or coincident redaction.

docs.title: 6. Directionality
docs.text: ΔR² = +0.024 (Luke from Matthew 0.219 vs Matthew from Luke 0.195; sign-flip p = 0.005) — but penalty-dependent (from +0.057 to 0), absent among the 30 length-balanced pairs (p = 0.38), and the statistic fails the positive control (Mark → Matthew p = 0.62; Mark → Luke p = 0.84). No directional inference is drawn.

docs.title: Conclusion
docs.text: The representation can be validated on known dependence, and once validated it measures the double tradition as closer than two-step Markan copying and at least as close as one-step copying, with part of the first contrast due to the kind of material. Most of this is visible in word overlap; the embedding's own contribution is a residual sensitivity to agreement across a change of wording. It does not tell who copied whom.

docs.title: The Synoptic Problem
docs.text: The Synoptic Problem is the challenge of explaining the extensive literary similarities and differences among the first three canonical gospels: Matthew, Mark, and Luke. They share common wording, order of events, and even parenthetical editorial comments, which strongly implies a literary relationship rather than merely independent reliance on oral tradition.

docs.title: The Two-Source Hypothesis (2SH)
docs.text:
The most widely accepted solution in modern scholarship is the Two-Source Hypothesis, which posits:

  1. Markan Priority: The Gospel of Mark was written first. Matthew and Luke independently used Mark as a primary narrative framework.
  2. The Q Source: Matthew and Luke also share about 235 verses of sayings material (the "Double Tradition") not found in Mark (e.g., the Lord's Prayer, the Beatitudes). The 2SH posits they independently drew this material from a lost written document of Jesus's sayings, designated Q (from the German Quelle, meaning "source").

docs.title: Farrer Hypothesis & Other Alternatives
docs.text: A significant minority of scholars reject Q, most notably through the Farrer Hypothesis. This model accepts Markan priority but argues that Luke used Matthew as a source (or vice versa), explaining the double tradition without postulating a lost document.

docs.title: How STCM Approaches the Problem
docs.text:
STCM does not attempt to "prove" Q. Instead, it tests whether the statistical distribution of the texts in high-dimensional embedding space is consistent with the Q hypothesis.

If Matthew and Luke both used Mark, the triple tradition shows exactly what written dependence looks like in the representation, in two forms: - Two-step copying: Matthew against Luke — two independent copies of one source. This is what the double tradition would be under the Two-Source Hypothesis. - One-step copying: Luke (or Matthew) against Mark — a copy against its source. This is what the double tradition would be under the Farrer Hypothesis.

We then measure the double tradition in the same space. The comparison that matters is the excess over each set's own floor: how much more alike true parallels are than unrelated passages of the same kind already are. On that measure the double tradition exceeds two-step copying in every configuration tested, and equals or exceeds one-step copying; part of the first contrast reflects the predominance of sayings in the double tradition. The triple tradition also shows that Matthew and Luke deviate from Mark in correlated ways (the minor agreements). None of this decides between Q and Luke's direct use of Matthew.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text: The entire STCM process is driven by run_pipeline.py. It is designed to be resumable and modular.

docs.title: Standard Run
docs.text:
To execute the entire pipeline from start to finish:

python run_pipeline.py

This will: 1. Load the SBLGNT texts and check the alignment tables 2. Load the embedding model lazily (only on a cache miss) 3. Calibrate on the Triple Tradition (45 pericopes) 4. Run advanced_analysis.py (Tables 1–4: floors, excess with CIs, nulls, shared deviation from Mark, Mark–Q overlaps, composite sensitivity, directionality, covariates, bootstrap) 5. Run baselines.py (lexical baselines), form_control.py (sayings vs narrative) and robustness.py (alternative encoders) 6. Draw Figures 1–5 7. Save all output to outputs/

To fill the embedding cache for all three encoder configurations first (the analyses then run without the model, except the sentence bootstrap):

python populate_cache.py

docs.title: Legacy steps
docs.text:
The retired composite Q-score, the latent-Q reconstruction and the old evaluation suite are not part of the article. They run only on request:

python run_pipeline.py --legacy

docs.title: Resuming from Cache
docs.text:
If a previous run was interrupted or you only want to re-run the final evaluation steps, use the --resume flag. It reads logs/STEP_LOG.md to determine the last completed step and picks up from there.

python run_pipeline.py --resume

docs.title: Overriding Configuration
docs.text:
STCM uses environment variables for configuration. You can change the behavior without editing code:

Change the embedding model:

# Linux / macOS
STCM_EMBEDDING_MODEL=bert-base-multilingual-cased python run_pipeline.py

# Windows PowerShell
$env:STCM_EMBEDDING_MODEL="bert-base-multilingual-cased"
python run_pipeline.py

Use the mean of the last four layers, or another model revision:

STCM_LAYERS=last4 python advanced_analysis.py
STCM_MODEL_REVISION=<git sha> python advanced_analysis.py

Increase log verbosity:

STCM_LOG_LEVEL=DEBUG python run_pipeline.py

docs.title: Understanding Outputs
docs.text: Look in the outputs/ directory for your results: - reports/advanced_analysis.md — Tables 1–4 and every embedding statistic in the article. - reports/baselines.md, reports/form_control.md, reports/robustness.md — Table 5, the form control and the encoder comparison (Appendix C). - reports/centred_cosine_ranking.csv — The per-pericope ranking (refs, stratum, form, theme, raw/centred cosine, excess, lengths, word overlap, Markan parallel, text-critical note). - reports/triple_tradition_table.csv, per_pericope_excess.csv, floor_table.csv, composite_sensitivity.csv, baseline_disagreements.csv — appendix tables. - reports/key_stats*.json — machine-readable numbers (the figure script and the tests read these). - figures/evaluation/fig1–fig5 — The article figure set. - reports/evaluation_summary.md, reports/q_score_distribution.csv, reports/system_validation.txt — legacy outputs (--legacy only).
